sections.title: 1. EBM Principles — Literature Search & Question Formulation

blocks.subtopic: Systematic literature-search methodology (cross-checking reference lists, hand-searching, grey literature)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf — the book's own syllabus outline (p.40) only lists that a search must cover multiple databases (Cinahl, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, PsycINFO, Pubmed, Sigle); the fuller methodology (cross-checking reference lists of retrieved studies, hand-searching unindexed material, writing to experts about missing studies, including grey literature such as conference abstracts/posters) is tested via the question bank only: A complete literature search must use multiple databases (not just one), cross-check the reference lists of retrieved studies, hand-search unindexed material, write to experts about missing studies, and include grey literature (conference abstracts/posters) — excluding conference posters as 'not peer reviewed' is the wrong strategy.

blocks.forTopic: Literature search completeness checklist (systematic review search strategy)
expansion: Search the reference lists of retrieved papers
Extend to papers in other languages

blocks.text: Mixing widely different study designs in one meta-analysis is discouraged (the 'apples and oranges' problem) — one cannot simply combine a cohort-study result with a rigorous RCT result to give a single pooled estimate; clear inclusion criteria and heterogeneity statistics guard against this.

blocks.subtopic: PICO question-framing format
blocks.note: Not stated anywhere in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search of the raw PDF) — the book's own syllabus (p.40) uses a different, five-part formula instead (PECO(t), see below). PICO itself is tested only via the question bank: **PICO** format structures a treatment question as Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome; useful for treatment questions but may not fit every clinical question.

blocks.text: The SPMM syllabus frames aetiology/exposure questions with **PECO(t)**: Patient, Exposure/intervention, Comparison, Outcome, (Time) — the book's own structure for this type of question, distinct from the treatment-question PICO format tested elsewhere.

blocks.subtopic: The '4 steps of EBP' framework (Ask / Acquire / Appraise / Apply)
blocks.note: This generic 4-step framework is not stated as such in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. The book's own syllabus outline (p.40) only echoes the first two steps under different headings ('Translation of clinical uncertainty into an answerable question', 'Systematic retrieval of the best available evidence') and is truncated before any equivalent to steps 3-4 appears. Tested via the question bank as: 1. Formulate an answerable question; 2. Track down the best available evidence; 3. Critically appraise the evidence; 4. Apply the evidence by integrating it with clinical expertise and patient values

blocks.subtopic: Choosing the comparator population when framing a side-effect question
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: When framing a question about a side effect (e.g. sexual dysfunction on **fluoxetine**), the most meaningful comparator population is patients not taking the drug at all, not patients on an alternative drug — this is what makes the risk figure meaningful to the patient.

blocks.subtopic: Impact factor (journal-level citation metric)
blocks.note: Not stated anywhere in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: Impact factor is a journal-level (not article-level) metric: it is calculated over a rolling three-year period as the average number of citations per published paper.

blocks.subtopic: Cochrane Library's component databases (CDSR / DARE / CENTRAL)
blocks.note: books/15-3-statistics.pdf names the Cochrane Library only in passing (as a search source, p.22, and in the syllabus database list, p.40) and never breaks it down into its component databases. Tested via the question bank: Cochrane Library = Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews + Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effectiveness (**DARE**, quality-appraised reviews published elsewhere) + Cochrane Controlled Trials Register (**CENTRAL**); it is not an alternative to Medline, and not every intervention trial is registered in it.

blocks.subtopic: CENTRAL (Cochrane Controlled Trials Register) as best resource for registered trials
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: **CENTRAL** (the Cochrane trials register) is currently the best single resource for locating registered clinical trials, including ongoing/unpublished ones.

blocks.subtopic: Researcher conflict-of-interest disclosure (honoraria from a competing drug's manufacturer)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: The single most important conflict of interest a researcher reviewing a drug must disclose is receiving honoraria for lecturing from a company that makes a competing drug.

items.text: Meta-analysis pooling 12 uncontrolled trials + 3 RCTs: the trap answer is that mixing designs makes a meta-analysis impossible. Correct: it only weakens it — best practice is two separate meta-analyses.
Impact factor is tested as if it measures the quality of a specific article — it is actually a journal-level, 3-year rolling citation average.
When framing a **PICO** comparator for discussing a side effect with a patient, the trap distractor is an alternative drug; the correct comparator is 'not taking the intervention at all'.
Candidates over-trust the Cochrane Library as covering all trials — it maintains **CENTRAL** but not every intervention trial is registered there, and it is not a substitute for Medline.

bullets.text: Mixing widely different study designs in one meta-analysis is discouraged (the 'apples and oranges' problem) — best practice is two separate meta-analyses.
**PECO(t)**: Patient, Exposure/intervention, Comparison, Outcome, (Time) — the SPMM syllabus's own structure for exposure/aetiology questions.

blocks.title: Key methodological questions for appraising each study type
rows: Was the process of treatment allocation truly random? Would participants have been able to know or guess their allocation? Were participants and researchers blinded to treatment group? Were outcomes assessed objectively? Were all randomised participants accounted for in the final analysis, and analysed in the group to which they were randomly allocated?

Is the study prospective or retrospective? Is the cohort representative of a defined group or population? Were all important confounding factors identified? Were exposures/treatments, confounders and outcomes measured accurately and objectively in all cohort members? Were there important losses to follow-up? Were participants followed up for a sufficient length of time?

Was the search comprehensive (not excluding articles by publication status or language, with publication bias assessed)? Were selected articles appraised and data extracted by two independent reviewers? Was sufficient detail given about the patients, interventions and outcomes of the primary studies? Was the quality of the primary studies assessed? Did the researchers assess the appropriateness of combining results into a summary measure?

Were the cases clearly defined and representative of a defined population? How were the controls selected, and were they drawn from the same population as the cases? Were study measures identical for cases and controls? Were measures objective or subjective, and is recall bias likely if subjective?

Was the study sample clearly defined? Was a representative sample achieved (was the response rate sufficiently high)? Were all relevant exposures, confounding factors and outcomes measured accurately? Were patients with a wide range of disease severity assessed?

Does the sample represent the full spectrum of patients with and without the diagnosis of interest? Was there a comparison with an appropriate gold-standard test? Did all patients receive both the test under evaluation and the gold-standard test? Were the tests performed independently, with assessors blinded to the gold-standard result? Were the cut-offs used to classify a positive test result clearly described?

blocks.subtopic: Generic named evidence-hierarchy schemes (I-1/I-2/II.../IV and meta-analysis>RCT>cohort>...)
blocks.note: books/15-3-statistics.pdf states only ONE named hierarchy — the Oxford Centre for EBM scheme (I, II, III-1, III-2, III-3, IV, V — see below). It does not state the alternative I-1/I-2/II-1/II-2/II-3/III/IV scheme, or the plain study-type ranking (meta-analysis > systematic review > RCT > non-randomised trial > cohort study > case-control study), both of which are tested via the question bank. Watch for exam questions naming a hierarchy scheme other than the Oxford one.

blocks.subtopic: Reporting-guideline map (CONSORT / PRISMA / STROBE / STARD / MOOSE / COREQ / QUOROM)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: CONSORT for RCTs; QUOROM (an early standard, since superseded by PRISMA) for meta-analyses of RCTs; PRISMA for systematic reviews; STROBE for observational studies (cohort/case-control/cross-sectional); STARD for diagnostic-accuracy studies; MOOSE for meta-analyses of observational studies; COREQ for qualitative research (interviews/focus groups).

source.file: question_bank/EBM/EMIs Evidence Based Medicine_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Guidelines (e.g. from **NICE**) are generated by a panel of stakeholders; being evidence-based, guidance is also value-based and dependent on local resource availability (cost) — the same evidence base can therefore yield different guideline recommendations in different settings.

blocks.subtopic: The Delphi method (expert-consensus technique)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: The Delphi method is an iterative, multistage group-facilitation technique used to transform expert opinion into a group consensus, commonly used to develop treatment guidelines.

blocks.title: Oxford Centre for EBM — Hierarchy of Evidence (an alternative named scheme)
rows: Systematic review of all relevant RCTs
Non-randomised comparative studies with concurrent controls (cohort, case-control, controlled interrupted time series)
Comparative studies with historical control, or uncontrolled interrupted time series

blocks.caption: Stem-and-leaf plot of a sample of scores (40,41 / 32,32,34,36 / 21,21,24,26,27,28,28 / 19): each row's stem (tens digit) is paired with one or more leaf digits (units), so each leaf represents one observation and the plot's shape shows the data's frequency distribution.

Path analysis diagram: three predictor variables (ANX, HSM, TAX) connected by curved double-headed correlation arrows (-0.26, 0.34, 0.26) and each with a one-headed path coefficient arrow (0.29, -0.38, 0.35) into outcome variable PNP, with an R-square of 0.41 and a disturbance term 'd' (error in measurement) feeding into PNP.

Scatter plot of ln(urea) (y-axis) against age (x-axis), each dot an individual observation, with a fitted regression line running through the points and a dotted vertical line marking the deviation (residual) between one observed point and the line.

Box-and-whisker plot of score (y-axis) across five diagnostic groups (No diagnosis, Anxiety, Depression, Comorbid depression and anxiety, Mixed anxiety-depression), each box showing the median line, upper/lower quartile (hinge) edges, upper/lower adjacent whiskers, and individual outlier/extreme-outlier points beyond 1.5x the quartile range (source: Das-Munshi et al, British Journal of Psychiatry 2008;192:171-177).

bullets.text: Guidelines (e.g. **NICE**) are produced by a stakeholder panel; being evidence-based, guidance is also value- and local-resource-based, so the same evidence can yield different recommendations in different settings.

blocks.text: Accuracy = all correct 'hits' / total = (**TP** + **TN**) / (**TP**+**TN**+**FP**+**FN**) — a coarser overall measure, with a maximum value of 100% (=1), same as sensitivity and specificity.

blocks.subtopic: Serial vs simultaneous (parallel) diagnostic testing
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Serial (sequential) testing — a second test only given if the first is positive — increases the specificity but decreases the sensitivity of the combined battery. Simultaneous (parallel) testing does the opposite: sensitivity rises, specificity falls, versus either test alone.

blocks.title: Diagnostic accuracy — core formulas
rows: Ability to correctly identify true positives among the diseased
Ability to correctly identify true negatives among the well
**LR** x pre-test odds (pre-test odds derived from prevalence)
Used to get post-test probability = odds / (odds + 1)
How much a negative result lowers disease odds

blocks.forTopic: Using sensitivity/specificity to rule disease in or out
expansion: SnNout — a test with high SeNsitivity, when Negative, helps rule **OUT** disease
SpPin — a test with high SPecificity, when Positive, helps rule **IN** disease

blocks.text: **EMI** trap: distinguishing 'the prevalence of disease among test-positives' (= **PPV** = **TP**/total positive) from 'how likely a positive result is given disease' (= likelihood ratio, sensitivity/(1-specificity)) — these produce different-looking but easily confused fractions from the same 2x2 table.

source.file: question_bank/EBM/EMIs Evidence Based Medicine_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Higher disease prevalence in the tested population raises positive predictive value (**PPV**); **PPV** rises and **NPV** falls as prevalence increases.

blocks.caption: Line chart 'Prevalence and Predictive Value' plotting positive predictive value and negative predictive value (y-axis, 0.00-1.20) against prevalence (x-axis, 0.1-0.5): positive predictive value rises with increasing prevalence while negative predictive value falls, the two lines crossing around a prevalence of 0.35-0.4.

blocks.text: Sensitivity, specificity and the likelihood ratio (**LR**+) are properties of the test itself and are not affected by disease prevalence in the population tested — only **PPV** and **NPV** are prevalence-dependent.

Lowering a diagnostic cut-off increases the number diagnosed (raises sensitivity, lowers specificity — more false positives); raising the cut-off does the reverse (fewer diagnosed, lower sensitivity, higher specificity). The cut-off may be shifted deliberately if the cost of false positives is judged higher than the cost of false negatives, or vice versa.

blocks.caption: Effect of moving a diagnostic cut-off between two overlapping distributions (no-disease vs disease): a lower cut-off (A) raises sensitivity at the cost of more false positives; a higher cut-off (B) raises specificity at the cost of more false negatives.

blocks.text: Raising a diagnostic cut-off from 3 to 4 on the **CAGE** reduces sensitivity but leaves specificity **UNCHANGED** in the sourced worked example — candidates often assume specificity must rise whenever sensitivity falls.
The best likelihood-ratio cut-off is not necessarily the one that maximises sensitivity or specificity individually — it is typically the central/median cut-off where the two trade off best.

Post-test odds = likelihood ratio x pre-test odds, where pre-test odds are derived from the pre-test probability (typically the prevalence in the studied population); post-test probability is then odds/(odds+1).

blocks.caption: Fagan/Bayesian nomogram (Method 2) with three scales — Pretest Probability, Likelihood Ratio, Posttest Probability — showing a worked example: a dashed line drawn from a pretest probability of 20% through a likelihood ratio of roughly 20 reads off a posttest probability of about 90%.

Likelihood Ratio Nomogram: three parallel vertical scales for Pre-Test Probability (%), Likelihood Ratio, and Post-Test Probability (%), used by drawing a straight line through a chosen pre-test probability and likelihood ratio to read off the resulting post-test probability.

blocks.subtopic: Worked Bayesian-updating numeric examples
blocks.note: books/15-3-statistics.pdf states the general pre-test-odds -> post-test-odds -> post-test-probability method (see above) without a worked numeric example. Two specific worked instances are tested via the question bank instead: (1) sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%, prevalence 10% -> LR+ = 8, post-test odds = 8/9, post-test probability approx 0.47; (2) pre-test probability 1/4 (odds 1/3), LR+ = 9.5 (from sensitivity 95%/specificity 90%) -> post-test odds = 3.16, post-test probability approx 0.75.

blocks.subtopic: Bayesian reasoning beyond basic post-test probability
blocks.note: The sourced questions only cover the mechanics of converting prevalence -> pre-test odds -> post-test odds/probability via a likelihood ratio. There is no coverage in this question bank of Bayesian priors more generally, decision-curve analysis, or how clinical judgement should combine with these calculations in practice.

blocks.text: A key methodological safeguard when validating a diagnostic test against a 'gold standard' is that the tests are performed independently, with assessors blinded to the gold-standard result.

A Receiver Operator Characteristic (**ROC**) curve plots sensitivity (true positive rate) on the y-axis against 1-specificity (false positive rate) on the x-axis; it is used to select the best cut-off and to compare two or more diagnostic instruments.

blocks.caption: ROC curve plotting sensitivity (y-axis) against 1-specificity (x-axis): a dashed curve bows toward the top-left corner, with a diagonal 'chance line' (the 45-degree line of no discrimination) running from (0,0) to (1,1) for comparison.

blocks.text: The area under the **ROC** curve (**AUC**) represents overall test accuracy; an **AUC** of 0.5 means the test cannot discriminate diseased from non-diseased any better than a coin toss — this is the performance of the diagonal 'line of no discrimination'.
**AUC** = 0.5 on an **ROC** curve is a trap for assuming any reported **AUC** implies good test performance — 0.5 means the test performs no better than chance (the diagonal line).
1-specificity, plotted on the **ROC** x-axis, is the false positive rate (since true negatives + false positives = ==100%== of non-diseased cases).
The best trade-off cut-off point sits at the 'elbow'/knee of the **ROC** curve, where sensitivity and specificity are jointly optimised even though neither is individually maximal.

blocks.caption: ROC curve annotated with successive cut-off points (1/2 through 9/10) plotted against a dashed chance line, alongside Table 3 listing sensitivity and (1-specificity) for each cut point of the SPNP scale, from <1 (sensitivity 1.00) down to >10 (sensitivity 0.00).

blocks.subtopic: Rasch measurement model / item misfit (scale validation)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (this EBM book covers diagnostic-test accuracy, not psychometric scale validation) — tested via the question bank: Deleting items that show significant misfit to a Rasch measurement model (e.g. from the 14-item to the 7-item Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale) improves construct validity, since the remaining items fit the underlying construct model better.

blocks.subtopic: Face validity trade-off when shortening a scale
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (this EBM book covers diagnostic-test accuracy, not psychometric scale validation) — tested via the question bank: A shortened scale can lose some face validity (a more restricted view of the construct) even while gaining ease-of-use, brevity, and reduced confounding by gender/age bias present in the deleted items.

blocks.subtopic: Test-retest reliability
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (this EBM book covers diagnostic-test accuracy, not psychometric scale validation) — tested via the question bank: Test-retest reliability is the method used to demonstrate that an instrument's scores remain stable over a defined period (e.g. 2 weeks).

blocks.subtopic: Summed interval-scale scores and parametric/non-parametric comparison
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (this EBM book covers diagnostic-test accuracy, not psychometric scale validation) — tested via the question bank: A summed interval-scale score (e.g. a short well-being scale) does not have meaningful physical units, even though it permits parametric comparison (t-test) or non-parametric comparison (Mann-Whitney U) depending on whether normality assumptions hold.

bullets.text: Accuracy = all correct 'hits' / total = (**TP** + **TN**) / (**TP**+**TN**+**FP**+**FN**), a coarser overall measure.
Higher disease prevalence raises **PPV** and lowers **NPV**.
Sensitivity, specificity and **LR+** are properties of the test, unaffected by prevalence — only **PPV**/**NPV** are prevalence-dependent.
Lowering a cut-off raises sensitivity/lowers specificity (more diagnosed); the cut-off may be shifted deliberately if the cost of false positives is judged higher than false negatives, or vice versa.
Post-test odds = **LR** x pre-test odds (from prevalence); post-test probability = odds/(odds+1).
Validating a new test against a 'gold standard' requires the two tests be applied **independently** of each other.
**ROC** curve plots sensitivity (y) vs 1-specificity (x); used to select a cut-off and compare diagnostic instruments.
1-specificity (the **ROC** x-axis) is the false positive rate, since **TN**+**FP** = ==100%== of non-diseased cases.
The best trade-off cut-off sits at the 'elbow' of the curve, even though neither sensitivity nor specificity alone is maximal there.

facts.label: AUC at line of no discrimination

blocks.text: Odds ratio (**OR**) is the cross-product ratio (a x d)/(b x c) from a 2x2 table; **OR** can only take values between 0 and infinity (no negative values), so confidence intervals for it require log transformation.
Relative risk cannot be calculated from a case-control study — incidence needs prospective observation, which only a cohort design provides; a case-control study can only produce an odds ratio.

blocks.subtopic: Case-control studies and temporal association
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Case-control studies cannot establish a temporal association between exposure and outcome (though dose-response patterns and confidence intervals for the **OR** can still be derived).

blocks.forTopic: What a case-control study cannot give you
blocks.mnemonic: The RAT stays out of case-control
expansion: R — Relative risk cannot be calculated
A — Attributable/population risk cannot be calculated
T — Temporal sequence between exposure and outcome cannot be established

blocks.title: What each observational design can and cannot calculate
rows: Odds ratio, dose-response pattern, **CI** for the **OR**
Relative risk, incidence, temporal association, true population prevalence (unless representatively sampled)
Sensitivity, specificity, **PPV**/**NPV** for the sample studied
True population prevalence, unless the sample is representative

blocks.subtopic: Population prevalence from a convenience-sampled case-control dataset
blocks.note: Not explicitly stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Given the same case/control exposure counts, one cannot determine true population prevalence from a convenience-sampled diagnostic/case-control dataset — this requires a genuinely representative sample.

blocks.subtopic: Case-control efficiency for studying a rare disease
blocks.note: books/15-3-statistics.pdf states the related 'rare disease assumption' (OR approximates RR when prevalence <5%) but not this specific efficiency rationale. Tested via the question bank: Case-control design is the most efficient choice when the disease under study is rare, even after exposure — a cohort design would need an impractically large sample to observe enough rare events.

blocks.subtopic: Nested case-control study design
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search — 'nested case-control' does not appear). Tested via the question bank: A nested case-control study identifies cases from a defined, prospectively followed cohort/register (e.g. **GPRD**) and samples matched non-cases from that same cohort using incidence density sampling (time-matched to the case's incidence date); this reduces recall and selection bias relative to a classic case-control design.

blocks.subtopic: Nested case-control and temporal association
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Despite being analysed retrospectively, a nested case-control study **CAN** support temporal-association claims because the underlying exposure/outcome data were recorded prospectively on the register before the analysis was done.

blocks.text: Nested case-control design is a trap for assuming all case-control designs share the same weaknesses: because the underlying register data were recorded prospectively, temporal association **CAN** be inferred here, unlike a classic case-control study.

blocks.subtopic: Nested case-control and residual confounding
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Even a carefully matched, register-based nested case-control design remains an observational design — confounding by an unmeasured third variable remains a threat to validity that cannot be experimentally excluded.

blocks.subtopic: Limits of causal inference from a case-control association
blocks.note: Not explicitly stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: From a case-control association alone, one cannot infer a causal relationship (e.g. 'antipsychotics cause hip fractures') — only the strength of association (**OR**, with **CI**) can be inferred; equally, no prescriptive clinical guideline can be derived from such cross-sectional/case-control work alone.

blocks.subtopic: Multicollinearity in multiple linear regression
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: Multiple linear regression can give unreliable/unstable significance estimates for individual predictors when two included independent variables are highly correlated with each other (multicollinearity) — they compete for statistical significance rather than acting as independent predictors.

blocks.text: Multicollinearity trap: when two independent variables in a multiple regression are highly correlated, individual predictors can appear falsely non-significant — this is not a sign the whole model or the outcome measure is invalid.

blocks.subtopic: Type 2 error risk from low exposure prevalence among cases
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: A low absolute prevalence of the exposure among cases (e.g. very few schizophrenia patients in a given cancer subgroup) increases the risk of a Type 2 error — a true association may be missed unless the sample is large enough.

blocks.text: **EMI** trap: the same raw 2x2 count table produces different valid statistics depending on whether it is labelled case-control, cohort, or cross-sectional — incidence rate and relative risk are only valid for the cohort framing, odds ratio for case-control, and prevalence for cross-sectional.

source.file: question_bank/EBM/EMIs Evidence Based Medicine_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: Relative risk is a classic case-control trap: it cannot be calculated from a case-control study (only odds ratio can), because retrospective sampling does not identify incidence.
Case-control studies are repeatedly tested as unable to establish temporal association between exposure and outcome, even when dose-response and **OR** confidence intervals are available.
Interpreting an **OR** of 5 from a case-control study as if it were a relative risk ('5 times greater risk') is wrong — the correct phrasing is in terms of odds, not risk.

'Point prevalence of the disease in the population' cannot be answered from a diagnostic-accuracy study built on a convenience (non-representative) sample of cases and controls — a common trap is assuming the case:control ratio approximates population prevalence.

blocks.text: Relative risk equal to or below 1.0 means no positive association between exposure and outcome — the risk in exposed persons equals or is below the risk in non-exposed persons.

blocks.caption: Figure 1: relationship between odds ratio and relative risk across a range of baseline incidence rates (I0) — the two only converge when the outcome is rare; at higher incidence the odds ratio diverges sharply above the relative risk.

Stacked bar chart comparing 'exposed' and 'non-exposed' groups: both bars share the same baseline incidence (not due to exposure, ~45), and the exposed bar carries an additional segment labelled 'incidence due to exposure (attributable risk)' bringing its total to ~78, while the non-exposed bar has no such additional segment.

blocks.subtopic: Attributable risk of 100% — interpretation
blocks.note: Not explicitly stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: If an exposure has an attributable risk of ==100%== for a disease, this means all incident cases of that disease are the result of that single exposure — a situation that is rarely, if ever, seen in practice.

blocks.subtopic: Population attributable fraction (PAF, Levin's formula)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search for 'PAF'/'Levin'). Tested via the question bank: PAF = Pe(RR-1) / [1+Pe(RR-1)], where Pe = proportion of population exposed. Worked example: RR = 10, prevalence of exposure 5% -> PAF approx 31%.

bullets.text: Relative risk cannot be calculated from a case-control study — incidence needs prospective observation, which only a cohort design provides.
Relative risk equal to or below 1.0 means no positive association between exposure and outcome.

blocks.subtopic: Why survival analysis is used instead of a t-test/ANOVA/chi-square
blocks.note: Not explicitly stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Survival methods measure 'time to an event' (e.g. discharge, death) and do not require a near-normal distribution, unlike the parametric assumptions of a t-test or **ANOVA**; they are preferable to a chi-square approach, which would lose information by dichotomising continuous time data.

blocks.text: In a Kaplan-Meier plot, the y-axis shows the proportion of subjects who have **NOT** yet reached the outcome of interest ('surviving'), and the x-axis shows time; the curve has a stepped appearance, with each step at a time of observation.

blocks.caption: Introductory Kaplan-Meier step curve (probability of surviving vs months in trial, 0-36 months) annotated with speech bubbles: the first event occurs at month 6, two events occur at month 18, three events occur at month 36 when the study is terminated (right-censored), leaving a probability of survival at the end of the trial of 20%.

blocks.text: The log-rank test assesses the effect of a single categorical variable on survival; Cox proportional hazards regression is needed to assess continuous variables (or multiple variables simultaneously), and assumes the hazard ratio is constant over time.

blocks.caption: Kaplan-Meier plot of probability of not developing major depressive disorder (y-axis, 0.85-1.00) against years (x-axis, 1-11) for smokers (dashed line) versus non-smokers (solid line): the non-smokers' curve stays above the smokers' curve throughout, both are left-censored (starting below 1.00) and right-censored (most subjects event-free at study end), and the smokers' curve ends around 84% survival with median survival time undeterminable.

blocks.text: Cox regression allows the effect of one variable on survival to be estimated while adjusting for others, distinguishing a variable's independent effect from one that is only associated with survival via another variable.

The median survival time is the time point at which the survival curve reaches ==50%==; if the curve is right-censored before reaching that point (follow-up ends too early), median survival time cannot be determined.

blocks.caption: Three annotated Kaplan-Meier-style survival curves on shared axes (probability of survival vs time period): one falls steeply below 0.5 early ('poor median survival: worse early prognosis but better later prognosis'), one stays flat near 1.0 for most of the period then drops ('representative median survival: no comparable differences'), and one starts by tracking the flat curve then drops sharply near the end ('impressive median survival: good early prognosis but poor later prognosis') — all three converge to a comparable survival probability by the end of the period.

blocks.subtopic: Evaluating Prognosis
blocks.note: Kaplan-Meier curves, the log-rank test, Cox proportional-hazards regression and median survival time are all covered in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (p.14) and are now cited there above, along with the book's own appraisal checklist for a prognostic study (see below). Still not covered anywhere in this book or its question bank: inception-cohort selection, prognostic-factor selection methodology, clinical prediction rules, or prognosis-specific biases such as lead-time or length-time bias — cross-check a core clinical epidemiology text for these.

blocks.text: Appraising a prognostic study: was the sample representative of a defined population (not filtered by referral/selection bias)? Was follow-up sufficiently long and complete? Were objective, unbiased outcome criteria used, ideally with assessors blinded to baseline predictors?

bullets.text: In a Kaplan-Meier plot, the y-axis shows the proportion of subjects who have **NOT** yet reached the outcome ('surviving'); the curve is stepped, each step at a time of observation.
Log-rank test assesses one categorical variable's effect on survival; Cox regression is needed for continuous/multiple variables (assumes a constant hazard ratio over time).
Cox regression estimates one variable's independent effect on survival while adjusting for others.
Median survival time = the point where the curve reaches ==50%==; cannot be determined if the curve is right-censored before reaching it.

Appraising a prognostic study: sample representative of a defined population (not filtered by referral/selection bias)? Follow-up sufficiently long and complete? Objective, unbiased outcome criteria, ideally with assessors blinded to baseline predictors?

blocks.subtopic: Randomisation and confounder balance (external validity)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Randomisation balances known and unknown confounders between groups at baseline; lack of randomisation (e.g. using self-selected volunteers) is a serious threat to external validity/generalisability.

blocks.subtopic: Baseline similarity attributable to randomisation, not blinding/ITT
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: The similarity of baseline characteristics between randomised groups is most likely attributable to randomisation itself, not to blinding or to intention-to-treat analysis (which act at later stages of the trial).

blocks.text: A key RCT-appraisal question is whether all randomly allocated participants were accounted for and analysed in the group to which they were randomly allocated, regardless of adherence — this is the intention-to-treat principle.

blocks.subtopic: ITT analysis with unequal dropout between arms
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Even when more patients drop out of one arm than another, an **ITT** analysis (analysing all patients per their original allocation) is the correct approach to preserve the value of randomisation.

blocks.subtopic: Crossover trial design
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Crossover trials are not subject to confounding by age, sex or other personal characteristics (each patient acts as their own control) and need fewer patients than parallel-group trials, but they are unsuitable for irreversible endpoints such as cure or death.

blocks.subtopic: n-of-1 trials — when most useful
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: n-of-1 trials are most useful when RCTs show a treatment is effective on average but a substantial proportion of patients do not respond, leaving doubt about whether this particular patient will benefit.

blocks.subtopic: n-of-1 trials — contraindications
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: n-of-1 trials are not appropriate to evaluate a treatment with only weak evidence for a potentially curative effect on a long-standing condition — and are impractical when a condition might fully resolve within the observation period.

blocks.subtopic: Placebo/active run-in phase before randomisation
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: A placebo (or active) run-in phase before randomisation is used to improve compliance — it can weed out non-compliers, wash out previous treatment, and establish a stable baseline before allocation.

blocks.subtopic: Odd/even date-of-birth quasi-randomisation
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: The odd/even last-digit-of-date-of-birth method of allocation is a quasi-randomisation technique and is the least adequate method of treatment allocation in a clinical trial.

blocks.subtopic: Cluster-randomised trials — effective sample size
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Cluster-randomised trials (randomising groups such as nursing-home units rather than individuals) reduce the effective sample size relative to individual randomisation of the same total N — higher power for a given N is achievable without cluster sampling.

blocks.text: Cluster-randomised trials need **MORE** participants than an individually-randomised trial of the same total N to achieve equivalent power, because intracluster correlation reduces the effective sample size.

blocks.subtopic: Intracluster correlation
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Intracluster correlation is the proportion of total outcome variability attributable to between-cluster (rather than within-cluster) differences; a high value means participants within a cluster behave like a single observational unit, shrinking the effective sample size toward the number of clusters.

blocks.subtopic: Equivalence trials — sample size requirement
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Equivalence trials require the largest sample size of all **RCT** types, since demonstrating a near-zero effect-size difference between treatments is statistically the hardest target to prove.

blocks.text: Equivalence trials are a trap for assuming smaller effect sizes need smaller samples — in fact equivalence trials (near-zero difference to demonstrate) require the **LARGEST** sample sizes of all **RCT** types.

blocks.subtopic: Repeat-testing/practice effect
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Repeated administration of the same or a similar test (e.g. a pre/post **CPD** quiz) can itself produce score gains through a repeat-testing/practice effect — this must be considered before crediting an intervention with the improvement.

blocks.subtopic: Trial participation effect in control arms
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Patients in the control arms of RCTs tend to do better than similar non-trial patients for reasons besides the specific intervention (a 'trial participation effect') — better clinician input, favourable selection, protocol adherence and a placebo/participation effect, but **NOT** simply higher medication potency.

blocks.title: Treatment-effect measures — NNT, NNH, ARR, RRR, RR, OR
rows: See the book's own worked example below (risperidone vs placebo, new-onset hyperlipidaemia)
Same formula as the causation/cohort **OR** — see 'Evaluating Causation'

blocks.text: **ARR** (book: **ABI**, absolute benefit increase) = |**CER** - **EER**| — the difference between the two groups' event rates.
**NNT** = 1/**ARR** — the number of patients who would need to receive the treatment for one of them to benefit.

blocks.caption: NNT Nomogram: three parallel vertical scales — Absolute risk in the absence of treatment (%), Relative risk reduction (%), and Number needed to treat — used by drawing a straight line through a chosen absolute risk and relative risk reduction to read off the number needed to treat.

blocks.text: **NNH** (number needed to harm) is calculated the same way as **NNT** but for an adverse outcome: **NNH** = 1/**ARR** for the harmful event.

blocks.caption: Bar chart of the rate of new-onset hyperlipidaemia (y-axis, 0-25%) comparing risperidone (20%) against controls (5%), the worked example behind an absolute risk increase of 15% and a number needed to harm of 7.

blocks.text: **RR** = **EER**/**CER** — the ratio between risk of the outcome in the treatment group and risk in the control group.
**RRR** (book: **RBI**, relative benefit increase) = **ABI**/**CER** — the absolute difference expressed as a proportion of the control-group risk.

blocks.subtopic: Worked ARR/NNT/NNH/RR/RRR examples
blocks.note: books/15-3-statistics.pdf (p.18) works through its own example instead: risperidone (experimental) vs placebo (control) for new-onset hyperlipidaemia — CER = 5%, EER = 20%, ARR (ABI) = 15%, NNH = 100/15 = 7, RR = EER/CER = 4, RRR (RBI) = 1-4 = -3 (i.e. a 3-fold relative increase in harm). The question bank instead tests: chlorpromazine 45% vs new drug 50% relapse -> ARR = 0.05; drug A 20/200 vs placebo 25/225 deaths over 3 years -> ARR = 1/90, NNT = 90, RR = 0.9, RRR = 0.1; NNH = 60 for suicidal acts on an antidepressant (back-calculated to 70/600 events); fluoxetine vs placebo in BDD improvement -> OR = 9.

blocks.subtopic: RRR looks larger than the corresponding ARR
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: **RRR** figures are usually far larger-looking than the corresponding **ARR**/risk-difference, which can make results seem more impressive than they are clinically — e.g. a ==50%== **RRR** may represent only a ==2%==->==1%== absolute drop.

blocks.text: **RRR** figures are deliberately tested because they look far more impressive than the corresponding **ARR** (e.g. a '==50%== **RRR**' framing can hide a ==2%==->==1%== absolute change) — always convert back to **ARR**/**NNT** before judging clinical significance.

blocks.subtopic: NNT inversely proportional to baseline event rate (constant RRR)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Assuming a constant **RRR**, **NNT** is inversely proportional to the baseline (control) event rate: a higher-risk population needs fewer patients treated per event prevented, and vice versa; **NNT** is also inversely related to **RRR** itself.

blocks.subtopic: Null value: 0 for difference statistics, 1 for ratio statistics
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: For relative risk reduction (**RRR**) and other difference-based statistics, the null value is zero — a ==95%== **CI** must not cross zero to be statistically significant. For ratio-based statistics (**RR**, **OR**), the null value is 1.

blocks.subtopic: p=0.05 and the 95% CI lower bound for RR
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: If a trial's exact p-value for a treatment effect is 0.05, the lower bound of the ==95%== **CI** for the relative risk is likely to sit right at 1.

blocks.subtopic: Sample size, point estimate, and CI width
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Increasing sample size while event rates stay the same does not change the point estimate of **RR** or **RRR** — it narrows the confidence interval around that same estimate, it does not shift it.

blocks.text: Increasing an **RCT**'s sample size while event rates stay identical is a trap for assuming the point estimate of **RR**/**RRR** changes — it only narrows the confidence interval, the point estimate stays the same.

blocks.subtopic: Wide CI spanning both harm and benefit
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: A wide ==95%== **CI** for **RRR** spanning both harm and benefit (e.g. -==28%== to +==49%==) means the trial has not actually resolved whether to offer the treatment, even if the point estimate looks favourable.

blocks.subtopic: Interpreting a 'negative' trial's CI upper bound
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: For an apparently 'negative' trial (p>0.05), check the upper bound of the **CI**: if it still contains an important treatment benefit, a real beneficial effect cannot be ruled out — only if the upper bound excludes any important benefit is the trial 'definitively negative'.

blocks.text: A trial with p>0.05 ('negative') is not automatically proof of no effect — check whether the upper **CI** bound still contains an important benefit before calling it 'definitively negative'.

blocks.subtopic: Pre-specified vs post-hoc subgroup analysis (single RCT)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Subgroup analysis results are more trustworthy when the subgroup hypothesis was specified before the study began, rather than generated after seeing the data.

blocks.subtopic: Composite endpoints
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Composite endpoints (e.g. death + **MI** + heart failure combined) reduce the required sample size and follow-up duration, but should not be used on the assumption that patients weight each component outcome equally — they usually do not.

blocks.subtopic: Surrogate/substitute endpoints
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: A surrogate/substitute endpoint is an easily measurable proxy used instead of the true patient-relevant outcome (e.g. a biomarker instead of survival); surrogates are attractive for feasibility but can be misleading. Activities-of-daily-living scores in a dementia trial are an example of a genuine (non-surrogate) patient-relevant outcome, not a surrogate.

blocks.subtopic: Hazard ratio as a weighted relative risk
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: The hazard ratio is essentially a relative risk weighted for the number of patients at risk over time in a survival analysis — useful when timing of onset, not just total count, matters.

blocks.subtopic: Why RCTs are stopped early
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: The most common reason RCTs are stopped early is the appearance of a large treatment effect that seems unlikely to be due to chance — not usually cost-saving or loss of investigator interest.

blocks.subtopic: Random error vs bias — sample-size dependence
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf. Tested via the question bank: Random error has a larger relative influence on the results of smaller studies (affecting reliability/reproducibility), whereas bias affects validity independent of sample size — a biased study can still be highly reproducible yet still wrong.

blocks.text: Adapting a trial's **NNT** to local practice: **PEER** (patient expected event rate, the baseline risk in the population actually being treated) replaces the trial's **CER** when the local population's baseline risk differs from the trial population's.

Interpreting **NNT** size: **NNT** close to 1 signals a highly effective treatment (e.g. antibiotics for a susceptible organism); **NNT** 2–5 signals an effective therapy for a common outcome; **NNT** ≥20 signals a marginal or preventive benefit.

bullets.text: A key RCT-appraisal question is whether all randomly allocated participants were analysed in the group to which they were randomly allocated, regardless of adherence — the intention-to-treat principle.
**ARR** (book: **ABI**) = |**CER** - **EER**|.
**NNH** = 1/**ARR** for the harmful event.
**RRR** (book: **RBI**) = **ABI**/**CER**.
Adapting **NNT** to local practice: **PEER** (patient expected event rate — local baseline risk) replaces the trial's **CER**.
**NNT** interpretation: close to 1 = highly effective; 2-5 = effective for a common outcome; ≥20 = marginal/preventive benefit.

blocks.subtopic: Statistical heterogeneity tests (Cochran's Q, I-squared, Galbraith/L'Abbe plots)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: Statistical heterogeneity is formally tested with Cochran's Q test and the I-squared statistic, and can be explored visually via forest plots, Galbraith plots and L'Abbe plots — using a second independent reviewer to select studies addresses selection bias, not heterogeneity, and is the odd one out among heterogeneity-assessment options.

blocks.subtopic: Interpreting a significant Cochran's Q result
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: A significant (low p-value) Cochran's Q result means the null hypothesis of 'all variability due to chance' is rejected, i.e. statistical heterogeneity is present; the test is sensitive to study sample sizes, so it can fail to flag true heterogeneity in small studies and can flag trivial heterogeneity in very large ones.

blocks.text: A significant Cochran's Q test is sensitive to the number/size of included studies: it may fail to flag true heterogeneity when studies are small, and flag trivial heterogeneity when studies are very large — don't treat its p-value as definitive on its own.

blocks.subtopic: Fixed-effect model assumption
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: A fixed-effect model assumes every included study is estimating the same true effect, with only within-study sampling variation causing observed differences (i.e. 'differences are due to chance').

blocks.text: Choosing between fixed-effect and random-effects models is about the **ASSUMPTION** of a single true effect vs accepting heterogeneity — not primarily about differences in methodological quality between studies.

blocks.subtopic: Random-effects model — when used, effect on CI width
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: A random-effects model is used specifically because heterogeneity exists between studies; it accepts that each study may be estimating a different underlying effect and incorporates between-study variance, generally widening the pooled confidence interval.

blocks.caption: Galbraith plot: standardised effect (y-axis) plotted against precision (x-axis) for 12 numbered studies as red dots, with a central line depicting the pooled effect size flanked by parallel +2SD and -2SD lines; studies 1, 9 and 11 fall outside the 2SD band and are flagged as outliers contributing to heterogeneity.

blocks.text: Inappropriate subgroup analyses: although the parent trials were individually randomised, that balance does **NOT** automatically extend to post-hoc subgroups carved out of the pooled data — subgroup findings should be treated as hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory.

blocks.subtopic: Effect-size measure for dichotomous meta-analysis outcomes (OR/RR, not LR)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: For dichotomous outcomes, effect size in meta-analyses is usually expressed as odds ratio or relative risk; likelihood ratio is a diagnostic-test measure and is **NOT** generally used to express meta-analytic effect size.

blocks.subtopic: Pooling continuous outcomes measured on the same rating scale
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: When individual studies measured a continuous outcome on the **SAME** rating scale, results can be combined directly using the weighted mean difference.

blocks.subtopic: Standardising continuous outcomes on different rating scales (SMD/Cohen's d)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: When individual studies measured a continuous outcome on **DIFFERENT** rating scales (e.g. **HAM-D** vs **BDI** for depression), results must first be standardised via the standardised mean difference (**SMD**, e.g. Cohen's d = difference in means divided by pooled **SD**) before pooling.

blocks.subtopic: Mean smaller than SD as a sign of skewed data
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: If a study's mean is smaller than its standard deviation, the underlying data are likely skewed — the researcher should consider a log transform or dichotomising the outcome rather than pooling the raw **SD**-based statistic.

blocks.text: When an included study's mean outcome is smaller than its own standard deviation, this signals skewed data that undermines simple **SD**-based pooling — a trap for assuming any continuous outcome can be pooled with a mean/**SD** approach.

blocks.subtopic: Failsafe N (Rosenthal's file-drawer estimate)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: Failsafe N is Rosenthal's estimate of the number of additional null/negative unpublished studies ('file-drawer' studies) that would be needed to reduce a significant meta-analytic result to non-significance.

blocks.text: A funnel plot (a measure of precision, e.g. sample size or standard error, plotted against a measure of effect size, e.g. Cohen's d/OR/RR) is used to detect the presence of publication bias via asymmetry — an obvious void on one side of the plot signals missing (unpublished, likely negative) studies.

blocks.caption: Funnel plot with no publication bias: a symmetrical, inverted-funnel scatter of sample size (precision) against effect size around the true effect size — larger studies cluster near the line, smaller studies scatter more widely on both sides.
Funnel plot showing evidence of publication bias: an asymmetrical scatter with an obvious void of missing (presumably unpublished, non-significant) small studies on one side of the true effect size.

blocks.text: The confidence interval of a meta-analysis's pooled effect size is explicitly **NOT** a valid method for detecting publication bias (that needs a funnel plot or failsafe N) — a common distractor in publication-bias questions.

blocks.subtopic: The '4 basic steps of meta-analysis' framework
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: 1: Literature search; 2: Establishing inclusion/exclusion criteria; 3: Recording data from individual studies; 4: Statistical analysis

blocks.subtopic: Typical stages of a systematic review (Higgins 2008)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: 1: Specification of evidence sought; 2: Identification of evidence; 3: Critical appraisal of evidence; 4: Synthesis of evidence

blocks.text: A thorough meta-analysis search strategy must look for unpublished data, for negative studies, and for publications in non-English languages, to minimise retrieval, language, and publication bias.

blocks.subtopic: RR=1/RR<1 significance still depends on the CI excluding 1 (meta-analysis framing)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: A risk ratio (**RR**) of 1 indicates no difference between groups; a risk ratio below 1 does **NOT** by itself mean 'no difference' — its statistical significance still depends on whether its **CI** excludes 1.

blocks.text: **NNT** can be derived from a meta-analysis's pooled control/experimental event rates (**CER**/**EER**) exactly as from a single trial — once **CER** and **EER** are known, **RR**, **RRR** and **ARR** follow, and from **ARR**, **NNT**.

blocks.subtopic: Worked meta-analysis NNT example
blocks.note: books/15-3-statistics.pdf states the general method (see above) without this specific worked example. Tested via the question bank: risperidone vs haloperidol for PANSS improvement, pooled ARR = 0.125 -> NNT = 8, with 95% CI for NNT = 7 to 10.

blocks.text: Appraising a meta-analysis (Guyatt et al.): was there a written protocol defining the question, outcomes, and inclusion/exclusion criteria in advance? Was the search comprehensive across languages and unpublished sources? Was study quality formally assessed before pooling?

A forest plot's pooled control/experimental event rates (**CER**/**EER**) can be reconstructed by summing each included study's event count and denominator across arms (e.g. pooled n and N added across studies) — useful for back-calculating an **NNT** from the plot alone.

A forest plot ('blobbogram') represents each study as a block/square at its point estimate, with a horizontal line showing its confidence interval; the size of the square reflects the study's weight in the pooled estimate, and a diamond/lozenge shows the pooled result.

blocks.caption: Forest plot from Wijkstra et al, Br J Psychiatry 2006;188:410-415, comparing antipsychotic-plus-antidepressant (AP+AD) against antipsychotic monotherapy (AP) across three study arms (Spiker et al 1985, Rothschild et al 2004 studies a and b), each shown as a point estimate with 95% CI and weight percentage, plus a pooled diamond total of RR 1.92 (95% CI 1.32-2.80) favouring AP+AD.

Forest plot 'Figure 1: Risk of relapse: odds ratios by drug type' showing five antidepressant drug classes (NARI, MAOI, Tricyclic, SSRI, Other) plus a pooled Total, each row giving number of trials, allocated-antidepressant and placebo event rates, and an odds-ratio point estimate with 95%/99% CI on a log scale — annotated with worked ABI/NNT calculations for MAOIs (ABI 65%, NNT 2) and overall treatment (ABI 23%, NNT 5).

expansion: S — Square size shows the study's Weight in the pooled estimate
W — Width of the horizontal line shows imprecision (wider = less precise)
A — Arrowhead means the **CI** extends beyond the plotted axis (very imprecise)
P — Pooled diamond/summary line at the bottom gives the overall effect

blocks.subtopic: Heterogeneity cannot be calculated for a single stand-alone trial
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: Heterogeneity, by definition, cannot be calculated for a single stand-alone trial in a forest plot — it only applies to the pooled set of studies.

blocks.text: Precision of a study's (or the pooled) estimate is reflected by the width of its horizontal line in a forest plot — a shorter line means more precise results; an arrowhead means the **CI**'s end cannot be shown within the plotted axis range (a sign of imprecision).

blocks.title: Recognising common EBM graph types
rows: Point estimate + **CI** per study (block size = weight)
Choosing a diagnostic cut-off / comparing tests (**AUC** = accuracy)

blocks.caption: L'Abbe plot: intervention event rate % (y-axis) plotted against control event rate % (x-axis) for 11 numbered trials, each drawn as a circle whose size represents that trial's sample size; a solid 'equal line' (RR=1) runs diagonally through the origin, and a dashed 'overall RR line' shows the pooled relative risk from the meta-analysis — trials below the equality line show better control-group event rates than intervention.

CONSORT-style RCT flow diagram: 547 patients randomised to OPUS (n=275) or ST (n=272) at baseline, with numbered and itemised losses to follow-up (refused/moved/not located/deaths, including suicides) shown at each stage, giving 205 (75%) of OPUS and 164 (60%) of ST followed up at 2 years, and 151 (56%) of OPUS and 150 (57%) of ST followed up at 5 years.

blocks.subtopic: Cost-effectiveness acceptability curve
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: A cost-effectiveness acceptability curve plots a range of willingness-to-pay thresholds against the probability that the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (**ICER**) falls below that threshold — it visualises statistical uncertainty in cost-effectiveness estimates.

blocks.subtopic: Ecological-fallacy scatterplot
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: A scatterplot of country-level (ecological) data, such as income inequality vs prevalence of mental illness across nations, risks the ecological fallacy if used to infer relationships at the individual level.

blocks.subtopic: Cumulative incidence by birth cohort (age-period-cohort design)
blocks.note: Not stated in books/15-3-statistics.pdf (confirmed by full-text search). Tested via the question bank: Plotting cumulative incidence (via Kaplan-Meier estimates) separately for each birth cohort demonstrates the combined effect of both age and calendar/birth year on incidence of a diagnosis — useful for showing trend-over-time alongside age effects.

bullets.text: Although parent trials were individually randomised, that balance does **NOT** automatically extend to post-hoc subgroups carved out of pooled meta-analysis data — subgroup findings are hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory.
A funnel plot (precision, e.g. sample size/SE, vs effect size, e.g. Cohen's d/OR/RR) detects publication bias via asymmetry — a void on one side signals missing (likely negative) studies.
A thorough search strategy must look for unpublished data, negative studies, and non-English-language publications, to minimise retrieval/language/publication bias.
**NNT** can be derived from a meta-analysis's pooled **CER**/**EER** exactly as from a single trial.
Appraising a meta-analysis (Guyatt et al.): was there a pre-specified written protocol? Was the search comprehensive (languages, unpublished data)? Was study quality formally assessed before pooling?
A forest plot's pooled **CER**/**EER** can be reconstructed by summing each study's event count and denominator across arms.
Forest plot ('blobbogram'): each study is a block at its point estimate with a CI line; block size = weight; the diamond/lozenge shows the pooled result.
Precision = width of a study's horizontal line (shorter = more precise); an arrowhead means the CI extends beyond the plotted axis.

blocks.text: The most important single component in developing a clinical guideline is having a systematically reviewed evidence base on which recommendations are built — even though guidance also incorporates value judgements and resource availability.
Guideline recommendations should not be prepared irrespective of local resources — being evidence-based, guidance is also value-based and dependent on local resource availability (cost).

Steps in producing a treatment recommendation: define the decision; specify the possible outcomes; use available evidence to link options to outcomes; incorporate value judgements; then consider local circumstances including resource availability.

Guidelines are most effectively implemented when developed by those who will use them, disseminated through a specific educational intervention, and reinforced by patient-specific reminders during consultations (e.g. filed in the notes).
The most effective single measure for getting clinicians to apply a new guideline in practice is using patient-specific reminders at the point of clinical contact.

blocks.subtopic: GRADE system & quality-of-evidence grading
blocks.note: The **GRADE** approach to grading quality of evidence and strength of recommendations is never mentioned anywhere in the 239 sourced questions, despite being a standard **EBM**/guideline topic. Recommend reviewing the **GRADE** handbook or **NICE**'s methods manual directly.

blocks.subtopic: Recommendations & Guidelines
blocks.note: Only 5 questions were sourced for this sub-bank. Coverage is limited to general principles of guideline development and implementation (evidence + values + resources, Delphi consensus); it does not cover formal recommendation-strength grading (e.g. **GRADE** strong/weak) or guideline-appraisal instruments (**AGREE** **II**).

blocks.text: Protocols demand strict adherence to a fixed procedure; guidelines are evidence-based recommendations intended to inform, not mandate, clinical decisions — deviation from a guideline is not itself a breach of care if clinically justified.

Decision analysis formalises a clinical choice as a tree: decision nodes (squares) branch into the available options, chance nodes (circles) branch into possible outcomes with their probabilities, and each end-point is assigned a utility value to calculate the option with the best expected value.

blocks.caption: Fig 1: a decision-analysis tree (folding back) — decision nodes (squares), chance nodes (circles) with outcome probabilities, and QALY-based utilities calculating the expected value of watchful waiting vs surgery for asymptomatic carotid stenosis.

blocks.text: Altman's nomogram reads off the sample size (or power) required for a study from a straight line joining the standardised difference (effect size) and the desired power/significance level — a graphical alternative to calculating sample size from first principles.

blocks.caption: Altman's nomogram: a diagonal ruled scale for standardised mean difference (effect size, 0.0-1.2) on the left, a required-sample-size (N) scale down the centre, and a significance-level/power pair of scales on the right (SIG LEVEL 0.0-0.05 and Power 0.05-0.995) — a straight line through a chosen effect size and power reads off the required sample size at the chosen significance level.

bullets.text: The single most important component of guideline development is a systematically reviewed evidence base — even though value judgements and resources also matter.
It is **NOT** appropriate to prepare recommendations irrespective of local resources — resource availability should modify a recommended action even with a strong evidence base.

Recommendation steps: define the decision → specify outcomes → link options to outcomes via evidence → incorporate value judgements → adjust for local resources — this is why guidance on the same evidence differs between countries.
Guidelines work best when developed by their own users, disseminated via a specific educational intervention, and reinforced by patient-specific reminders during consultations.
The single most effective measure for guideline uptake is a patient-specific reminder at the point of clinical contact.

Protocols mandate strict procedure; guidelines are evidence-based recommendations meant to inform, not mandate — deviating from a guideline is not automatically a breach of care if clinically justified.

Decision analysis models a clinical choice as a tree: decision nodes (squares) branch into options, chance nodes (circles) branch into probability-weighted outcomes, each end-point given a utility value to find the option with the best expected value.
Altman's nomogram: a graphical tool that reads off required sample size (or power) from a line joining the standardised difference (effect size) and desired power/significance level.

mindMap.label: EBM Principles — Literature Search & Question Formulation

children.label: 'Apples and oranges' — don't mix widely different study designs in one meta-analysis
**PECO(t)**: Patient, Exposure/intervention, Comparison, Outcome, (Time)
**PICO**: Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome (treatment questions)
4 steps of EBP: Ask -> Acquire -> Appraise -> Apply
Impact factor = journal-level, 3-year rolling citation average
Cochrane Library = **CDSR** + **DARE** + **CENTRAL** — not a substitute for Medline
**PICO** side-effect comparator trap — correct comparator is 'not taking the drug', not an alternative drug
Key appraisal questions by study type
RCT: was allocation truly random, blinding used, all participants analysed by allocation (ITT)?
Cohort: prospective or retrospective, confounders identified, losses to follow-up?
Systematic review/meta-analysis: comprehensive search, independent dual review, quality of primary studies assessed?
Diagnostic accuracy: compared to gold standard, blinded assessors, clear cut-offs?
Named evidence-hierarchy schemes vary — watch for a scheme other than the Oxford one

Reporting-guideline map: **CONSORT** (RCTs), **PRISMA** (systematic reviews), **STROBE** (observational), **STARD** (diagnostic accuracy), **MOOSE** (observational meta-analyses), **COREQ** (qualitative)

children.label: Guidelines are evidence-based **AND** value/resource-based — the same evidence can yield different guidance in different settings
Delphi method — iterative expert-consensus technique for developing guidelines
Oxford Centre for EBM — Hierarchy of Evidence
I: Systematic review of all relevant RCTs
II: At least one properly designed RCT
V: Expert opinion without critical appraisal
Diagnostic accuracy — core formulas
Sensitivity = **TP**/(**TP**+**FN**)
Specificity = **TN**/(**TN**+**FP**)
**PPV** = **TP**/(**TP**+**FP**) — rises with prevalence
**LR**+ = Sensitivity/(1-Specificity) — unaffected by prevalence
**EMI** trap: **PPV** (prevalence among test-positives) vs likelihood ratio (Sens/(1-Spec)) — easily confused fractions from the same 2x2 table

source.file: question_bank/EBM/EMIs Evidence Based Medicine_ Attempt review.pdf

children.label: Lowering a cut-off raises sensitivity/lowers specificity (more false positives); may be shifted deliberately by the relative cost of false positives vs false negatives
Raising the **CAGE** cut-off from 3 to 4 reduces sensitivity but leaves specificity **UNCHANGED** in the sourced worked example
Post-test odds = **LR** x pre-test odds; post-test probability = odds/(odds+1)
**ROC** curve plots sensitivity vs 1-specificity; **AUC** of 0.5 = no better than chance (the diagonal line)
Serial testing raises specificity/lowers sensitivity of a test battery; simultaneous (parallel) testing does the opposite
Odds ratio = (a x d)/(b x c) cross-product; ranges 0 to infinity, so **CI**s need log transformation
Relative risk cannot be calculated from a case-control study — only a cohort design gives incidence
Case-control studies cannot establish temporal association between exposure and outcome
What each observational design can/cannot calculate
Case-control: can get **OR**, dose-response, **CI** for **OR**; cannot get **RR**, incidence, temporal association
Cross-sectional/convenience-sampled diagnostic study: can get sensitivity/specificity/**PPV**/**NPV** for the sample; cannot get true population prevalence unless representative
Nested case-control study **CAN** support temporal-association claims — the underlying register data were recorded prospectively
Multicollinearity trap: two highly correlated predictors in a regression can appear falsely non-significant — not a sign the whole model is invalid
Attributable risk formulas (cohort studies)
**AR** = **EER** - **CER**; example 25/200 vs 10/200 over 8 years -> **AR** = 0.075
**PAR** = **AR** x proportion of population exposed; example **AR**=20/100, ==25%== exposed -> **PAR** = 1/20
**PAF** (Levin's formula) = Pe(**RR**-1)/[1+Pe(**RR**-1)]; example **RR**=10, prevalence ==5%== -> **PAF** approx ==31%==
Survival analysis handles 'time to event' without needing near-normal distributions (unlike t-test/**ANOVA**) and avoids dichotomising time (unlike chi-square)
Kaplan-Meier plot: y-axis = proportion **NOT** yet reaching the outcome ('surviving'); the curve is stepped at each observed event
Log-rank test assesses one categorical variable's effect on survival; Cox regression is needed for continuous/multiple variables (assumes a constant hazard ratio)
Cox regression estimates a variable's independent effect on survival, adjusting for others
Median survival time = point where the curve reaches ==50%==; cannot be determined if right-censored before that point
Appraising a prognostic study: representative sample, sufficient/complete follow-up, objective outcome criteria with blinded assessors
Treatment-effect measures
**ARR** (book: **ABI**) = |**CER** - **EER**|
**RRR** (book: **RBI**) = 1 - **RR** (equivalently **ARR**/**CER**)
Intention-to-treat: all randomly allocated participants analysed in the group they were allocated to, regardless of adherence
Cluster-randomised trials need **MORE** participants than individual randomisation of the same total N — intracluster correlation shrinks the effective sample size
Equivalence trials require the **LARGEST** sample sizes of all **RCT** types — a near-zero difference is the hardest target to prove
**RRR** looks far more impressive than the corresponding **ARR** (e.g. ==50%== **RRR** can hide a ==2%==->==1%== absolute change) — always convert back to **ARR**/**NNT**
A 'negative' trial (p>0.05) is not proof of no effect — check whether the upper **CI** bound still contains an important benefit
Null value = 0 for difference statistics (e.g. **RRR**); null value = 1 for ratio statistics (**RR**, **OR**)
**NNT** interpretation: close to 1 = highly effective; 2-5 = effective for a common outcome; ≥20 = marginal/preventive benefit
Statistical heterogeneity tested with Cochran's Q and the I-squared statistic; explored visually via forest, Galbraith and L'Abbe plots
A significant Cochran's Q is sensitive to study size — may miss true heterogeneity in small studies, flag trivial heterogeneity in very large ones
Fixed-effect model assumes one true effect across studies; random-effects model accepts heterogeneity — the choice is about this assumption, not study quality
Random-effects model is used when heterogeneity exists between studies and generally widens the pooled **CI**
Funnel plot (precision vs effect size) detects publication bias via asymmetry — a void on one side signals missing (unpublished) studies
Failsafe N (Rosenthal) = number of additional null 'file-drawer' studies needed to reduce a significant result to non-significance
The **CI** of a pooled effect size is **NOT** a valid method for detecting publication bias — that needs a funnel plot or failsafe N
Forest plot ('blobbogram'): each study is a block at its point estimate (size = weight) with a **CI** line; the diamond shows the pooled result
The single most important component of guideline development is a systematically reviewed evidence base
Guidance is evidence-based **AND** value-based, dependent on local resource availability (cost)
Steps: define the decision -> specify outcomes -> link options to outcomes via evidence -> incorporate values -> adjust for local resources
The single most effective measure for guideline uptake is a patient-specific reminder at the point of clinical contact
Protocols mandate strict procedure; guidelines inform (not mandate) decisions — deviation isn't automatically a breach of care
Decision analysis tree: decision nodes (squares) branch into options, chance nodes (circles) branch into probability-weighted outcomes, each end-point given a utility value
